Options: A) System software that manages hardware and software resources
Explanation: The OS is the core software that manages CPU, memory, storage, I/O devices, and provides an interface for users and applications.

Options: A) Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, and iOS
Explanation: OS examples: Microsoft Windows, Apple macOS, Linux distributions, Android (mobile), iOS (Apple mobile).

QuestionText: The part of the OS that is always in main memory and manages core functions is
Explanation: The kernel is the core of the OS: it manages memory, processes, I/O, and hardware communication directly.

QuestionText: The interface that allows users to interact with the OS using a command line is called
Explanation: CLI: text-based interface where users type commands (e.g. MS-DOS prompt, Linux terminal/bash shell).

QuestionText: The interface that uses icons, windows, and a mouse is called
Explanation: GUI: visual interface with icons, menus, and windows (e.g. Windows Desktop, macOS Finder). Easier for beginners than CLI.

QuestionText: Which of the following is an example of a CLI OS?
Explanation: MS-DOS was a command-line operating system with no graphical interface, used in early PCs.

QuestionText: The OS function that allocates memory to running programs and manages it is
Explanation: Memory management: OS allocates RAM to processes, handles virtual memory, and ensures programs don't overwrite each other.

QuestionText: The OS function that decides which process gets CPU time and when is
Explanation: Process/CPU scheduler: allocates CPU time to processes using algorithms (FCFS, Round Robin, SJF) for efficient multitasking.

QuestionText: A file system organises data into
Options: A) Files and directories (folders) on storage devices
Explanation: File system (FAT32, NTFS, ext4): organises data into files and directories, manages storage space allocation.

QuestionText: Windows uses NTFS as its primary file system. NTFS stands for
Explanation: NTFS (New Technology File System): default Windows file system; supports large files, permissions, encryption, journaling.

QuestionText: The process of loading the OS into memory when a computer starts is called
Explanation: Booting: the startup sequence that loads the OS from storage into RAM so the computer can operate.

Options: A) Volatile memory that temporarily stores data currently in use
Explanation: RAM: fast, volatile (loses data on power off) memory used for active programs and data; temporary working memory.

Options: A) Non-volatile memory that stores permanent firmware (e.g. BIOS)
C) A type of hard disk
Explanation: ROM: non-volatile memory containing pre-programmed instructions (BIOS/UEFI) that don't change on power off.

Options: A) Disk space used as an extension of RAM when RAM is full
Explanation: Virtual memory: the OS uses a portion of the hard disk as additional RAM when physical RAM is insufficient (page file/swap space).

Options: A) A program in execution (with its own memory space and resources)
Explanation: Process: an active instance of a program being executed; has code, data, stack, and system resources allocated to it.

Options: A) Multiple processes to run concurrently (or seemingly so) on one CPU
B) Only one program at a time
Explanation: Multitasking: the OS rapidly switches between processes, giving the illusion of simultaneous execution on a single CPU.

QuestionText: A deadlock in an OS occurs when
Options: A) Two or more processes are stuck waiting for resources held by each other
B) A process runs too fast
Explanation: Deadlock: circular waiting — Process A holds resource 1 and wants resource 2; Process B holds resource 2 and wants resource 1. Both stuck.

Options: A) A centralised database storing OS and application configuration settings
Explanation: Registry: hierarchical database in Windows storing system and application settings, user preferences, and hardware configurations.

QuestionText: Which key combination opens Task Manager in Windows?
Options: A) Ctrl+Alt+Delete (then select Task Manager) or Ctrl+Shift+Esc
Explanation: Task Manager: shows running processes, CPU/memory usage, and allows ending unresponsive programs.

QuestionText: The Control Panel in Windows is used to
Options: A) Configure system settings, hardware, and software
Explanation: Control Panel (Settings in Windows 10/11): central location for system configuration (display, sound, network, user accounts).

Options: A) Free, open-source OS used on servers, desktops, and embedded systems
Explanation: Linux: open-source kernel by Linus Torvalds (1991). Distributions: Ubuntu, Fedora, Debian. Powers most web servers.
Android (Google, 2008): built on the Linux kernel. The world's most widely used mobile OS.

QuestionText: The BIOS/UEFI is firmware stored in
Explanation: BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) or UEFI: firmware in ROM that initialises hardware during boot and passes control to the OS bootloader.

Options: A) Software that allows the OS to communicate with hardware devices
Explanation: Device drivers: programs that translate OS commands into device-specific instructions (e.g. printer driver, graphics driver).

QuestionText: A 'process state diagram' in OS shows transitions between
Options: A) New, Ready, Running, Waiting/Blocked, and Terminated states
Explanation: OS processes cycle through: New → Ready → Running → Waiting (I/O) → Ready again → Terminated.

Options: A) Memory into fixed-size frames/pages to allow non-contiguous allocation
Explanation: Paging: physical memory divided into fixed frames; logical memory into pages. Eliminates external fragmentation.

Options: A) Memory into variable-size logical segments (code, data, stack)
D) Memory into RAM and ROM
Explanation: Segmentation: divides process memory into logical segments of variable sizes, reflecting program structure.

Options: A) Application programs request services from the OS kernel
Explanation: System calls (open, read, write, fork, exec): the interface between user-space programs and the kernel.

Options: A) The user interface layer (CLI or GUI) that interacts with the kernel
Explanation: Shell: the user-facing interface that interprets commands and calls kernel functions (bash, zsh for CLI; Windows Explorer for GUI).

Options: A) The OS saves the state of one process and restores another to the CPU
Explanation: Context switch: CPU saves current process state (registers, PC) to PCB and loads the next process's state. Enables multitasking.

Options: A) Excessive page swapping causes the system to spend more time swapping than executing
Explanation: Thrashing: system spends more time moving pages between RAM and disk than executing processes; caused by too little RAM.

Options: A) Files and directories in the current directory
Explanation: ls (list): displays files and directories. ls -l shows detailed listing; ls -a shows hidden files.

QuestionText: The 'cd' command in command line changes
Explanation: cd (change directory): navigates between directories. cd .. moves up one level.
mkdir (make directory): creates a new folder. E.g. mkdir Projects creates a folder named Projects.
cp source destination: copies files. cp -r copies directories recursively.
rm: deletes files permanently in Linux (no undo). rm -r removes directories recursively. Use with caution.
Linux permissions: r (read), w (write), x (execute). Set for owner, group, and others (e.g. rwxr-xr-x).
chmod (change mode): modifies read/write/execute permissions for files and directories.

Options: A) Reorganises scattered file fragments to improve read speed
Explanation: Defragmentation: reorganises fragmented files on HDD into contiguous blocks for faster access. Not needed for SSDs.

QuestionText: A file extension tells the OS and user
Options: A) What type of file it is and which application can open it
Explanation: File extension: .docx (Word), .xlsx (Excel), .jpg (image), .mp3 (audio), .exe (executable).

Options: A) Prepares it for use by writing a new file system (erases all data)
Explanation: Formatting: creates a new file system on a storage device. Low-level format zeros sectors; high-level writes file system.

Options: A) Network connectivity to a host by sending ICMP echo requests
Explanation: ping hostname/IP: sends ICMP packets to test if a host is reachable and measures round-trip time.

Options: A) IP address and network configuration of the computer
Explanation: ipconfig/ifconfig: shows network interface details including IP address, subnet mask, default gateway.

Options: A) Which process gets CPU time and in what order
Explanation: CPU scheduler: selects which ready process gets CPU next using algorithms (FCFS, SJF, Round Robin, Priority).

Options: A) A signal that tells the CPU to stop current tasks and handle an urgent event
B) A type of error only
Explanation: Interrupt: hardware or software signal that preempts the CPU to handle high-priority events (keypress, I/O completion, timer).

QuestionText: The file allocation table (FAT) in FAT32 file system
Options: A) Keeps track of which disk clusters belong to each file
Explanation: FAT (File Allocation Table): a table on disk listing which clusters are used by each file and which are free.

Options: A) Publicly available source code that anyone can view, modify, and distribute
Explanation: Open source: source code is available for anyone to view, modify, and distribute. Examples: Linux, Firefox, LibreOffice.

Options: A) Software owned by a company/individual with restricted use and source code
Explanation: Proprietary software: owned by developer, source code is secret, users must agree to license (Windows, MS Office, Adobe).

Options: A) Jobs in batches without user interaction during processing
B) One job at a time interactively
Explanation: Batch OS: queues jobs and runs them without user intervention. Efficient for large repetitive tasks (payroll processing).

QuestionText: A real-time OS (RTOS) is used in
Options: A) Time-critical systems requiring guaranteed response times (e.g. medical devices, aircraft)
Explanation: RTOS: strict timing guarantees. Used in embedded systems: pacemakers, anti-lock brakes, aircraft controls.
